title: COSA: Context-aware Output-Space Adapter for Test-Time Adaptation in Time Series Forecasting
claim: A small adapter turns a frozen model's prediction into a corrected one using recent ground-truth context, and adapts online from observed errors.
layout: 1 panel, left-to-right; module row above a time series, feedback loop in red
description: A single wide diagram with a time-series plot at the bottom and a block diagram above it. The x-axis is split into Context Window, Input Look-back Window and Prediction. The context window is a gray ground-truth curve cut into dotted segments. A gray arrow carries these segments to a μ (mean) node. From there, gray arrows go through Context Vector, Linear Layer and Gating inside a green dashed box labeled COSA. A boxed Base Model takes the look-back window. caption: Overview of COSA operation showing the context-aware gated linear adapter architecture with input processing, linear transformation, gating mechanism, and output correction for test-time adaptation.
abstract: Deployed time-series forecasters suffer performance degradation under non-stationarity and distribution shifts. Test-time adaptation (TTA) for time-series forecasting differs from vision TTA because ground truth becomes observable shortly after prediction. Existing time-series TTA methods typically employ dual input/output adapters that indirectly modify data distributions, making their effect on the frozen model difficult to analyze. We introduce the Context-aware Output-Space Adapter (COSA), a minimal, plug-and-play adapter that directly corrects predictions of a frozen base model. COSA performs residual correction modulated by gating, utilizing the original prediction and a lightweight context vector that summarizes statistics from recently observed ground truth. At test time, only the adapter parameters (linear layer and gating) are updated under a leakage-free protocol, using observed ground truth with an adaptive learning rate schedule for faster adaptation. Across diverse scenarios, COSA demonstrates substantial performance gains versus baselines without TTA (13.91$\sim$17.03\%) and SOTA TTA methods (10.48$\sim$13.05\%), with particularly large improvements at long horizons, while adding a reasonable level of parameters and negligible computational overhead. The simplicity of COSA makes it architecture-agnostic and deployment-friendly. Source code: https://github.com/bigbases/COSA_ICLR2026
